query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys under tribo-corrosion, the overall degradation is governed by a dynamic competition between the mechanically induced removal of a protective, compositionally enriched passive (oxide) layer and its rapid re‐formation via selective oxidation. This process is further localized by micro‐galvanic interactions between different phases or compositional regions, which accelerate local corrosion when the passive layer is disrupted by wear.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy exhibiting a nearly homogeneous single-phase or dual-phase microstructure that is capable of forming a coherent, self-healing oxide/passivation layer with regions enriched in noble elements or phases that differ in Volta potential.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to combined sliding wear and corrosion in an aggressive electrolyte (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl) under controlled mechanical loading that periodically removes or damages the protective oxide film.
generation.conditions: Tests performed under identical tribological conditions with a corrosive medium, comparing specimens with identical bulk chemistry but differing in surface oxidation state or phase distribution due to prior thermal/chemical treatments.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and integrity of a passive oxide layer, whose selective development on one phase over another creates local galvanic cells that modulate corrosion rates.
generation.mechanism: During tribological contact, mechanical wear continuously removes the protective passive film. Its removal exposes the substrate to accelerated corrosion; however, selective oxidation driven by the alloy’s composition rapidly reforms the film. The coexistence of phases with differing electrochemical potentials results in micro-galvanic coupling, which localizes and intensifies corrosion at sites where the film is most disrupted. The overall degradation rate reflects the balance between the rate of film removal (by wear) and film reformation (by oxidation) modulated by these galvanic interactions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline alloy with a less robust passive layer, an HEA that forms a more stable, rapidly re-passivating oxide will exhibit lower total degradation. In a controlled comparison, the wear component may remain similar, but the corrosion component (and thus coupled tribo-corrosion degradation) will be reduced. However, if the passive film is too brittle or its reformation kinetics are too slow relative to wear, both wear and corrosion degradation can become exacerbated.
generation.baseline: A matched HEA sample that does not develop the enhanced protective oxide (or lacks favorable micro-galvanic partitioning), resulting in either continuous exposure of the substrate or premature film breakdown under identical tribological conditions.
generation.boundary: This prediction should hold in environments where the electrolyte is aggressive enough to cause corrosion but where the alloy’s oxidation kinetics can still keep pace with the mechanical removal. It may fail in conditions of extreme mechanical stress (overwhelming passive film formation) or if the environment inhibits re-oxidation (e.g., very low oxygen partial pressure), which would decouple the interdependence of wear and corrosion.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative balance between wear-induced film removal and the kinetics of re-passivation, as well as the precise role of micro-galvanic interactions at the microscale, are not fully quantified in current studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA specimens with identical bulk compositions. Pre-treat one set to enhance passive film formation (e.g., via a controlled oxidation heat treatment) and leave the other set untreated. Subject both sets to identical tribo-corrosion tests in a defined corrosive electrolyte under controlled sliding wear conditions. Monitor in situ wear track evolution, film continuity (via surface spectroscopy), weight loss, and local electrochemical potential mapping.
measurements: Wear track depth and morphology (via profilometry/SEM)
Surface film integrity and composition (via XPS or AES)
Mapping of local Volta potentials (via scanning Kelvin probe)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the enhanced passive film does not result in a statistically significant decrease in the corrosion component of degradation (or if micro-galvanic differences do not correlate with localized corrosion rates) relative to the untreated baseline under identical wear conditions, then the hypothesis that re-passivation and micro-galvanic interactions govern the coupled tribo-corrosion response is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The attractiveness of refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as structural materials stems from their outstanding mechanical properties, thermal stability, wear resistance and corrosion performance in hostile environments [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ]. Recently, refractory high-entropy alloys have received significant attention in relation to high-temperature application in aerospace, defense, and nuclear power generation industries [ [6] ]. In fact, they were designated to replace traditional Ni-based super-alloys in applications such as gas turbines, heat exchangers, aerospace propulsion components, rocket engine nozzle [ [7] ]. HEAs are multicomponent systems that are composed from a small number of principal elements. They are usually composed from at least five elements with individual atomic concentrations that range between 5% and 35%. HEAs can produce solid phase solutions, mainly due to their configurational entropy and ability to be adequately synthesized [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
